title: Two worlds: kernel mode and user mode
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain why the processor runs your code in a restricted mode, name three things your program genuinely cannot do itself, and read the boundary in a running system.

blocks.text: Your program cannot talk to a disk. It cannot send a packet. It cannot even end itself — not directly. Every one of those actions belongs to the kernel, and your code reaches them by asking. This is not a convention that programs politely follow. It is enforced by the processor, in hardware, on every single instruction.
The processor has a privilege setting

A modern CPU always runs in one of at least two modes. In kernel mode, every instruction is available: change the page tables, talk to a device, disable interrupts. In user mode, those instructions do not execute — attempting one does not misbehave quietly, it traps into the kernel, which then decides what to do with your process. Usually it kills it.

blocks.title: root is not kernel mode — this trips up almost everyone
blocks.text: In the Linux course you learned that root can do anything a user can be permitted to do. That is a permission check inside the kernel, and a root process still runs in user mode. It still cannot touch physical memory or a device register directly; it just gets 'yes' to requests that another user gets 'no' to. Kernel mode is a hardware state. root is a number in a process's credentials.
You have already seen the boundary enforced

When a C program dereferences a wild pointer and dies with a segmentation fault, that is this mechanism firing. The process touched an address the kernel had not mapped for it; the hardware trapped; the kernel looked at the fault, found no legitimate mapping, and delivered a fatal signal. The crash you saw in the C course was the boundary doing its job.

blocks.caption: Three things only the kernel can do for you
lines: /* 1. Open a file — the kernel checks permissions and tracks the handle */
/* 2. Get memory from the system — the kernel maps pages into you */
/* 3. End the process — the kernel reclaims everything you were holding */

blocks.text: Each of those lines looks like an ordinary function call in your source. None of them is. Each one crosses into the kernel, does its work at a privilege level your code never holds, and returns. The next lesson is about exactly how that crossing happens.

A crossing is not free. The processor switches mode, the kernel saves your registers, validates what you passed, does the work, and restores you. That overhead is why a program that reads a file one byte at a time is dramatically slower than one that reads it in large blocks — the work is the same, but the number of crossings is not. You will measure this yourself in the capstone.

blocks.title: This is why the kernel interface is small and stable
blocks.text: Linux has a few hundred system calls, and their behaviour changes very slowly, because everything ever compiled depends on them. It is a deliberately narrow, deliberately boring door. Narrow doors are easier to guard — which is the same reason the security modules in the last module of this course hang off exactly this boundary.

blocks.title: See the two worlds in a running system
steps: Run: cat /proc/self/status | grep -E 'Name|Pid|Uid'    (a process describing itself through the kernel)
Run: ps -eo pid,user,comm | head -12                   (some of these are kernel threads)
Run: ps -eo pid,comm | grep -E '\[.*\]' | head        (names in brackets are kernel threads — no user-mode code at all)
Run: cat /proc/uptime && cat /proc/loadavg             (values the kernel exposes as files)
Run: dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/null bs=1 count=100000 2>&1 | tail -1
Run: dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/null bs=100000 count=1 2>&1 | tail -1
Compare the two times: identical bytes moved, wildly different number of crossings
blocks.expected: The last two commands move the same 100,000 bytes. The first does it in about 200,000 crossings — a read and a write per block — and the second in two. The time difference is the cost of the boundary, and it is the single most useful number to have a feel for in this whole module.

cheatsheet: The CPU runs in user mode or kernel mode — enforced in hardware, per instruction
User mode: only your mapped memory, no devices, no privileged instructions
Kernel mode permits privileged control, but ordinary accesses still follow page mappings and protections such as SMEP/SMAP; kernel code can deliberately manage those mappings and devices
root is a permission inside the kernel, NOT kernel mode
A segfault is this boundary rejecting an unmapped address
Crossing the boundary costs time — batch your I/O instead of byte-at-a-time
/proc is the kernel exposing its own state as files
Process names in [brackets] are kernel threads

checkpoint.prompt: A process is running as root. Which statement is true?

choices.A: It can execute privileged CPU instructions directly
choices.B: It runs in kernel mode and can touch any physical address
choices.D: It still runs in user mode

checkpoint.explanation: Root only changes which requests the kernel approves. Kernel mode is a hardware privilege state. root is a credential the kernel checks when deciding whether to grant a request. A root process makes the same system calls as anyone else — it just gets 'yes' more often.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is reading a file one byte at a time so much slower than reading it in 64KB blocks, even though the total bytes are identical?

choices.A: Each read crosses into the kernel, and that fixed overhead dominates
choices.B: The disk firmware reads single bytes more slowly than full blocks
choices.C: Single-byte reads bypass the page cache, always hitting the device
choices.D: The C library refuses to buffer small reads, so they go straight to disk

checkpoint.explanation: Same bytes, vastly more boundary crossings. Each crossing saves and restores state and re-validates arguments, and that fixed cost is paid once per call.

checkpoint.prompt: Your program dereferences a pointer to an address it never allocated. What actually happens?

choices.A: The C compiler catches it at build time
choices.B: The kernel silently allocates the page
choices.C: The program reads whatever another process had there
choices.D: The hardware traps to the kernel

checkpoint.explanation: Finds no valid mapping and delivers a fatal signal. This is the user/kernel boundary enforcing itself. Option C describes exactly what memory protection exists to prevent.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does Linux keep the number of system calls small and their behaviour stable for decades?

choices.A: Adding a new system call requires new hardware support in every CPU
choices.B: Each one must fit entirely inside a single CPU register
choices.C: The CPU enforces a hard limit on how many system calls can exist
choices.D: Every compiled program depends on them staying stable and narrow

checkpoint.explanation: It is the contract between every program ever built and the kernel. It is also the attack surface, so keeping it narrow serves compatibility and security at the same time.
